title: Pauri 14: trusting, the path is clear
hookLine: mannai: by trust the path is not blocked and one walks with honor (Japji 14)
tomorrow: Pauri 15: trusting, the door of freedom

cards: There's an email you haven't answered. A call you keep meaning to make, a doctor's appointment you keep not booking, an apology sitting in your versions. It's been there so long it feels like a wall.
Every day you walk up to it, look at it, and turn around. Then one day you just do it, and the strange thing is how small it was. The wall was mostly fear.
Once you step, the road behind it is ordinary road. Pauri 14 says that for the one who trusts, the path isn't blocked.

teach.h: MAARAG — THE ROAD. THAAK — A BLOCK.
teach.b: Pauri 14 has four short lines, each beginning with mannai, by trusting. The first, in the original: mannai maarag thaak na paae. Maarag is the road, the way.
Thaak is a block, a barrier, something that stops you. By trusting, the road meets no barrier.
The second, in paraphrase: by trusting, one goes forth with honor, openly, in full view. Pat is honor, and the picture is of someone who doesn't have to sneak.
The third: by trusting, one doesn't wander off down side roads. Commentators read this as not being pulled here and there by every passing path, ritual or fashion.
The fourth: by trusting, one is bound to dharma, to right living. Then the refrain: such is the Name of the Stainless One, known only to the one who trusts it in the mind.
So the stanza draws a road: clear, walked openly, not drifted from, tied to doing right. Notice what it doesn't promise. Not easy, not short, not free of hills.
Just not blocked. The pauri doesn't list the barriers. Many readers hear in them the ones fear builds: hesitation, doubt, the sense that you'll be seen and judged.
On that reading, trust takes those down. Yesterday, trust's first gift was awareness. Today's is movement.
Wake up, then walk: Japji keeps building step on step.

how: Pauri 14 is recited as part of Japji Sahib in the Sikh morning Nitnem; many Sikhs hear its four mannai lines as a description of living openly and rightly out of trust.

o: a block or barrier in the way
the road, the way you walk
a lamp you light at night

games.q: the road of Pauri 14 — tap the pairs.

s: Pauri 14 promises the road will be easy and short
it promises the road won't be blocked, not that it won't have hills.
Pauri 14 says the one who trusts is bound to dharma
its fourth line ties trusting to right living.
in Pauri 14, the one who trusts goes forth openly, with honor
pat is honor: nothing to hide, nothing to sneak around.

games.q: you're on the road of trust, and side roads keep calling. what does Pauri 14 say the one who trusts does?
o: tries every side road to be sure.
stops walking until they go quiet.
games.why: by trusting, one doesn't drift off down side roads; commentators hear every passing path, ritual or fashion.

practice: Think of one step you've been avoiding, just the first one: the first line of the email, the number you need to dial. Picture yourself taking it, simply, in full view.
Notice where fear sits in your body as you picture it, and breathe into that spot.

wordCard.voice: Maarag. The road, the way: by trusting, it meets no barrier, and one goes forth with honor, bound to dharma.

orig.note: Gurmukhi, Japji Pauri 14: by trusting, the road meets no barrier.

carryVoice: Your line: the way opens. The road may have hills, but no wall. That's day one hundred eighty-five.

sources.ref: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 3 (Japji, Pauri 14, line 1)
